# SpatialFiltering

## `ESFModel`

    ESFModel

An eigenvector spatial filtering fit, returned by [`fit_esf`](@ref).

Spatial structure is absorbed by adding selected eigenvectors of the
doubly-centred weight matrix to the design as synthetic regressors, chosen
stepwise. Because they are orthogonal to the intercept and to each other,
the covariate coefficients stay interpretable as ordinary regression
coefficients — the appeal of the method over a lag model.

Inspect the chosen basis with [`selected_eigenvectors`](@ref).

!!! note
    Selecting zero eigenvectors is a valid outcome, not a failure: it means
    the residuals were already free of spatial autocorrelation.

## `REESFModel`

    REESFModel

A random-effects eigenvector spatial filtering fit, returned by
[`fit_re_esf`](@ref).

Instead of selecting eigenvectors stepwise as [`fit_esf`](@ref) does, this
keeps the whole screened pool and shrinks every coefficient towards zero,
governed by one variance ratio `theta = tau2/sigma2` estimated by profile
REML. That avoids the model-selection variance stepwise search introduces.

!!! warning
    The reported residual Moran coefficient is for the *conditional*
    residual and is **supposed to be substantially negative** — do not
    compare it against zero. Subtracting the fitted spatial term leaves the
    remainder in the orthogonal complement of the retained eigenvectors,
    which is itself negatively autocorrelated. Compare it against
    `moran_reference`, the closed-form expectation stored on the model.

## `STPCAResult`

    STPCAResult

Spatio-temporal principal components, as returned by [`stpca`](@ref).

### Fields
- `values`: eigenvalues of `E`, descending. Each is the value of the
  maximised objective, `Var(U_k) · A(Aγ_k)`, for its own component.
- `vectors`: the directions `γ_k`, one per column, orthonormal.
- `scores`: `n × K`, the units' positions on each component, `A γ_k`.
- `variance`: `Var(U_k) = γ_k' S γ_k`, the first factor of the objective.
- `autocorr`: the second factor — Geary's `C` or Moran's `I` of that
  component's scores.
- `proportion`: `λ_k / Σ|λ|`. For `:geary` every eigenvalue is
  non-negative, so this is the ordinary share; for `:moran` it is signed.
- `coefs`: `n × B`, the column-centred basis coefficients `A`.
- `measure`: `:geary` or `:moran`.
- `n_basis`, `n_features`, `interval`, `varnames`: what the expansion used.

See also [`stpca`](@ref), [`feature_contributions`](@ref),
[`component_weight`](@ref).

## `SpatialEigen`

    SpatialEigen

A screened eigenvector basis for spatial filtering, as returned by
[`spatial_eigenvectors`](@ref).

### Fields
- `values::Vector{T}`: eigenvalues of `Ω = M Wᵤ M`, in descending order.
- `vectors::Matrix{T}`: the corresponding eigenvectors, one per column. Columns
  are orthonormal and each sums to zero.
- `moran::Vector{T}`: each eigenvector's Moran coefficient, `(N/S₀)λᵢ`.
- `S0::T`: the sum of all weights, `Σᵢⱼ wᵢⱼ`.
- `N::Int`: the number of spatial units.

Pass an instance as the `eigen_basis` keyword of [`fit_esf`](@ref) or
[`fit_re_esf`](@ref) to reuse one decomposition across several fits.

## `component_groups`

    component_groups(m)

The positive and negative components of `m`, as index vectors into its
spectrum, in the order the reference reports them.

Under `measure = :moran` the sign of an eigenvalue is a substantive result,
not a numerical detail: a positive one is a **global** component, where
linked units carry similar scores, and a negative one is a **local**
component, where a unit's score is surrounded by unlike ones. The reference
orders the positive group by decreasing eigenvalue and the negative group by
decreasing *absolute* eigenvalue — the strongest local structure first — and
this returns `(positive = …, negative = …)` in that order. `m.values` itself
is sorted descending throughout, so the negative group appears there in the
opposite order.

Under `measure = :geary` the construction is non-negative definite, so the
negative group is empty up to rounding and the whole spectrum is the
positive one.

!!! note "Zero eigenvalues are in neither group"
    `B = p · n_basis` directions exist, but at most `min(n - 1, B)` carry
    variance. The rest have eigenvalues at rounding level and are excluded
    from both groups by `tol`.

## `component_weight`

    component_weight(m, k, t)

The vector weighting function `u_k(t)` of component `k`, evaluated at `t`:
a `length(t) × p` matrix whose column `j` is the weight the component puts
on feature `j` at each moment.

A spatio-temporal component is a direction in coefficient space, and this
is what that direction looks like as a function of time — the functional
analogue of a loading. Feature `j` is the one the component is reading at
moment `t` when `|u_kj(t)|` is the largest of the `p` entries.

See also [`feature_contributions`](@ref).

## `feature_contributions`

    feature_contributions(m, k; n_grid = 512)

How much each feature contributes to component `k`, as the share of the
area under `|u_kj(t)|` over the expansion interval:

```math
A^*_j = A_j \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^p A_i, \qquad
A_j = \int_I |u_{kj}(t)|\,dt
```

Returns a `Vector` of `p` shares summing to one, in the order of
`m.varnames`. The feature with the largest share is the one the component
is mostly made of, which is the reading the reference reports alongside the
component scores — a component is only interpretable once you know which of
the `p` series it is tracking.

The integral is taken by the trapezoid rule on `n_grid` points, since
`|u_kj|` has corners wherever `u_kj` crosses zero and no closed form.

See also [`component_weight`](@ref).

## `fit_esf`

    fit_esf(X, y, W; family=:gaussian, max_eigenvectors=20, criterion=:moran, ...)

Eigenvector spatial filtering (Griffith, 2003). Selected eigenvectors of the
doubly-centred `W` enter as extra regressors, absorbing the spatial
autocorrelation so the remaining coefficients can be read as aspatial:

```math
g(\mu) = \alpha + X\beta + E_{sel}\gamma
```

`family` is `:gaussian` (OLS), `:poisson`, `:logit`, or `:negbin`; the last three
are fit by IRLS. The negative binomial's dispersion is re-estimated between IRLS
passes, by its own maximum likelihood (`dispersion=:mle`, the default) or by the
method of moments of Chun et al. (2016) (`dispersion=:moments`). This makes ESF
usable wherever a GLM is, which parametric SAR/SEM cannot match.

Eigenvectors are added greedily. `criterion=:moran` picks, at each step, the
candidate that most reduces the absolute Moran coefficient of the residuals
(Pearson residuals for GLM families); `criterion=:aic` picks the one that most
reduces AIC. Selection stops at `max_eigenvectors`, when no candidate improves
the criterion, or — under `:moran` — once `|MC|` falls below `moran_tol`.

`min_moran_ratio` screens the candidate pool to eigenvectors with
`MCᵢ/max(MC) ≥ ratio` (default 0.25, the usual positive-SA screen). Pass a
precomputed [`SpatialEigen`](@ref) as `eigen_basis` to reuse one decomposition
across several fits.

Cost is `O(max_eigenvectors × n_candidates)` model fits, so keep the pool bounded
for GLM families.

### Inference after selection

The standard errors treat the selected basis as if it had been fixed in
advance. It was not: the eigenvectors were chosen on the same `y`, by a
greedy search over the whole candidate pool. Coverage of a nominal 95%
interval for the covariate slopes is therefore below 95% whenever
eigenvectors are actually selected. Over 400 replications at `N = 64` with
SAR(0.6) errors, about 5 eigenvectors selected per fit:

| | β₁ | β₂ |
|---|---|---|
| nominal | 95% | 95% |
| measured | 91.5% | 90.5% |

With no spatial autocorrelation almost nothing is selected and coverage is
right (94.8%, 94.5%). So read the slopes as point estimates whose
intervals are mildly optimistic, and treat the gap as the cost of letting
the data pick the basis. [`fit_re_esf`](@ref) avoids the problem by
shrinking a fixed basis instead of selecting from it, and its intervals
are not subject to this caveat.

### The GLM families

All four log-likelihoods match the corresponding `Distributions.logpdf`
to 1e-10, and IRLS reaches the actual maximum: at the returned `β̂` the
score of an independently written log-likelihood vanishes to 1e-13 and a
Newton step moves by 1e-16.

`vcov` is the inverse of the IRLS information `X′WX`. The log and logit
links are canonical for the Poisson and the Bernoulli, so that is also
the observed Hessian; the coverage those two reach is in the table below.

The log link is **not** canonical for NB2, so `X′WX` is the expected
information there and genuinely differs from the Hessian. That is the
right choice — the NB2 information matrix is block diagonal in `β` and
`α`, so estimating the dispersion does not inflate `Var(β̂)`.

The dispersion itself is estimated by maximum likelihood: the root of the
profile score for `α` at the current `μ`, found by Newton on `log(1/α)`
within a maintained bracket. The alternative, `dispersion=:moments`, is
the Pearson moment estimate of Chun et al. (2016), kept because that is
the scheme the method was published with. The MLE is the more precise of
the two at every sample size: at a true `α = 0.5` over 3000 samples its
root mean squared error is 0.199 against the moment estimate's 0.285 at
`N = 81`, and 0.046 against 0.067 at `N = 1500` — about a third off
throughout — and it is the closer of the two on roughly two samples in
three. Its median bias at `N = 81` is −8.7% against −16.2%.

The moment estimate also reports a dispersion on the positivity floor far
more often: on the `N = 81` coverage design below it does so for 5.6% of
fits against the MLE's 0.7%. Those fits keep the working weights at their
Poisson values, and their slope intervals cover 13 to 19 points worse
than the same scheme's other fits.

Coverage of a nominal 95% slope interval at `N = 81`, over 6000
replications on the design described above:

| | β₁ | β₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Poisson | 93.1% | 93.2% |
| logit | 94.5% | 94.7% |
| negbin, `:mle` | 93.3% | 92.6% |
| negbin, `:moments` | 92.2% | 91.6% |

So the dispersion is no longer what holds the negative binomial back: on
`:mle` it covers as well as the Poisson does. What the three count and
binary families still have in common is the post-selection effect
described above under *Inference after selection* — the mean standard
error is 0.92 of `β̂`'s actual sampling standard deviation for every one
of them, `:moments` and `:mle` alike — and that, not the dispersion, is
what the last two points are.

!!! note "Identification"
    The design has to have full column rank. `X` goes in without an
    intercept, since one is added, and no covariate may be a linear
    combination of the others. A design that fails this throws an
    `ArgumentError` naming the offending column, rather than failing
    inside the linear algebra or returning an arbitrary split of one
    coefficient across two.

## `fit_re_esf`

    fit_re_esf(X, y, W; min_moran_ratio=0.25, n_candidates=nothing, varnames=nothing)

Random-effects eigenvector spatial filtering (Murakami & Griffith, 2015):

```math
y = X\beta + E\gamma + \varepsilon, \quad
\gamma \sim N(0, \tau^2\Lambda), \quad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I)
```

Rather than selecting eigenvectors discretely, every positive-eigenvalue
eigenvector is retained and its coefficient shrunk toward zero, with the
shrinkage governed by the single variance ratio `θ = τ²/σ²` estimated by profile
REML. This sidesteps the model-selection variance of stepwise ESF.

Because `E` has orthonormal columns, `V = σ²(I + θEΛE')` inverts in closed form —
its eigenvalues are `1 + θλₗ` inside `span(E)` and 1 outside — so each REML
evaluation is O(NL), not O(N³). The decomposition itself is still O(N³).

Only positive-eigenvalue eigenvectors are used, the standard choice for positive
spatial autocorrelation, and `min_moran_ratio` screens them further to
`MCᵢ/max(MC) ≥ ratio`.

!!! note "Reading the residual Moran coefficient"
    `moran_final` is the Moran coefficient of the *conditional* residual
    `y - Xβ̂ - Eγ̂`, and **it is expected to be substantially negative — do not
    compare it against zero.** Subtracting `Eγ̂` removes the positively
    autocorrelated directions, leaving a residual that lives mostly in the
    orthogonal complement of `span(E)`; a vector drawn at random from that
    complement has Moran coefficient

    ```math
    \frac{N}{S_0}\cdot\frac{-S_0/N - \sum_l \lambda_l}{N - 1 - L}
    ```

    which is reported as `moran_reference`. On correctly specified data with
    `N = 121` and `L = 40` this reference is −0.304 and the fitted residual lands
    near −0.24, i.e. slightly *less* negative than chance. A `moran_final` close
    to or above `moran_reference` is the healthy case; one far below it suggests
    the random effects are absorbing noise, as does an `edf` (effective degrees
    of freedom, `P + Σ θλ/(1+θλ)`) approaching `N`.

!!! note "Identification"
    The design has to have full column rank. `X` goes in without an
    intercept, since one is added, and no covariate may be a linear
    combination of the others. A design that fails this throws an
    `ArgumentError` naming the offending column, rather than failing
    inside the linear algebra or returning an arbitrary split of one
    coefficient across two.

## `fourier_basis`

    fourier_basis(times, n_basis; interval = nothing)

Evaluate the first `n_basis` orthonormal Fourier basis functions at `times`,
returning a `length(times) × n_basis` matrix.

The basis on an interval of length `L` is `1/√L`, then `√(2/L)·sin(2πkt/L)`
and `√(2/L)·cos(2πkt/L)` for `k = 1, 2, …`, taken in that order and
truncated at `n_basis`. It is orthonormal with respect to `∫ over the
interval`, which is what lets the functional inner product `⟨u, X⟩` be
computed as the plain dot product of coefficient vectors.

The reference's construction is one constant plus whole sin/cos pairs, so
an odd `n_basis` is the natural choice — 5 is the reference's own, and the
default here. An even `n_basis` is allowed and still orthonormal, but it
ends on a sine with its cosine missing, which is a basis the reference does
not use.

`interval` defaults to `times` padded by half the mean spacing at each end.
The padding is not cosmetic: a Fourier basis is periodic, so an interval
running exactly from the first observation to the last forces the fitted
curve to take the same value at both, which is a constraint the data have
no reason to satisfy. Krzyśko et al. observe 2002–2018 at `t = 0.5, 1.5,
…, 16.5` and expand on `[0, 17]`, which is this default.

See also [`stpca`](@ref).

## `moran_coefficient`

    moran_coefficient(y, W)

Moran coefficient `(N/S₀) · (z'Wz)/(z'z)` for `z = y - ȳ`, where `S₀` is the sum
of all weights. The bare statistic with no inference — use
`SpatialDiagnostics.moran_global` when you need a p-value.

## `selected_eigenvectors`

    selected_eigenvectors(m::ESFModel)

Indices of the selected eigenvectors (into the candidate pool) with their Moran
coefficients, plus the residual Moran coefficient before and after filtering.

## `spatial_eigenvectors`

    spatial_eigenvectors(W; n_candidates=nothing, min_moran_ratio=0.0)

Eigendecomposition of the doubly-centred weight matrix
`Ω = (I - 11'/N) Wsym (I - 11'/N)`, following Griffith (2003).

The eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal and uncorrelated, and each carries
Moran coefficient `MCᵢ = (N/S₀)λᵢ`. Eigenvectors with large positive eigenvalues
describe positive spatial autocorrelation patterns; large negative eigenvalues
describe negative ones. Results are sorted by eigenvalue, descending.

An asymmetric `W` (e.g. row-standardised) is symmetrised as `(W + W')/2` so the
eigenvalues are real.

The constant vector is removed by construction rather than by discarding an
eigenvector afterwards: with `Q` an orthonormal basis of `1`'s orthogonal
complement, `Q'ΩQ = Q'WsymQ`, so eigendecomposing the reduced
`(N-1)×(N-1)` matrix and mapping back as `E = QV` yields vectors that are
orthonormal *and* exactly mean-zero. Decomposing `Ω` directly would not: its
null space is multi-dimensional, the solver may return any rotation within it,
and the constant direction then smears across several near-zero eigenvectors
that are each partly collinear with the intercept.

`n_candidates` keeps only the leading eigenvectors; `min_moran_ratio` keeps those
with `MCᵢ / max(MC) ≥ ratio`, the usual screen for positive-SA filtering (0.25 is
a common choice). Both are applied after sorting.

Dense `eigen` is O(N³) — intended for moderate N.

## `stpca`

    stpca(X, W; measure = :geary, n_basis = 5, times = axes(X, 3), kwargs...)

Spatio-temporal principal components: directions that maximise the product
of a functional principal component's variance and the spatial
autocorrelation of the scores it produces.

`X` is `n × p × T` — `n` spatial units, `p` features, `T` observation times
— or `n × T` for a single feature. Each unit-feature time series is first
expanded in `n_basis` orthonormal Fourier functions by least squares, giving
an `n × B` coefficient matrix `A` with `B = p · n_basis`; the components are
then found in that coefficient space, so time enters through the expansion
and space through `W`.

With `S = A'A/n`, a functional principal component `U = γ'α` has estimated
variance `γ'Sγ`, and its scores across units are `y = Aγ`. Writing the
spatial measure of those scores as a ratio of quadratic forms, the product
of the two factors collapses to a single eigenproblem:

```math
\hat{\mathrm{Var}}(U)\,\mathcal{A}(A\gamma) = \gamma' E \gamma,
\qquad \|\gamma\| = 1
```

so the components are the orthonormal eigenvectors of `E`, and each
eigenvalue *is* the product being maximised. For `measure = :geary`,
`E = ((n-1)/(2na))·A'B*A` where `a = Σᵢⱼwᵢⱼ` and `B*` is the symmetrised
contiguity matrix of Geary's ratio; for `measure = :moran`,
`E = (n/(a·n))·A'·((W + W')/2)·A`.

### Keywords
- `measure`: `:geary` (default, Krzyśko et al. 2023) or `:moran`.
- `n_basis`: Fourier functions per feature. Must not exceed `T`.
- `times`: observation times, `1:T` by default.
- `interval`: expansion interval, padded by half the mean spacing by
  default — see [`fourier_basis`](@ref).
- `varnames`: feature names, used in `feature_contributions`.

!!! warning "The two measures do not order the spectrum the same way"
    Moran's `I` is large when linked units agree, so `measure = :moran`
    puts smooth, global structure at the top and leaves the negative
    eigenvalues — the local components — at the bottom. That split is
    sharp: over 800 planted draws a smooth field landed on the first
    component in 73–87% of them and a high-contrast field on the last in
    72–86%, and neither ever landed at the wrong end.

    Geary's `C` runs the other way, large when linked units differ, so
    maximising `Var · C` demotes smooth structure — in those same draws a
    smooth planted field was never the first `:geary` component. But the
    `:geary` ordering is **not** the reverse of the `:moran` one: the
    high-contrast field led only 7–34% of the time, because the objective
    is a product and a moderate-`C` component with large variance outranks
    a high-`C` component with little. Read the `:geary` ordering as
    "variance weighted by dissimilarity", not as "most dissimilar first".

    The whole spectrum is returned either way, so both ends are always
    available. What is not safe is reading "the first component" without
    saying which measure produced it. `docs/AUDIT.md` has the rates.

!!! note "Why `E` is non-negative definite under `:geary`"
    `γ'Eγ` is a variance times a Geary ratio, and both factors are
    non-negative, so every eigenvalue is too — `rank(E)` of them positive
    and the rest zero. Under `:moran` the second factor can be negative,
    which is exactly the global/local split the eigenvalue signs carry.

### Examples
```julia
m = stpca(X, W; n_basis = 5, times = 0.5:1:16.5, interval = (0.0, 17.0))
m.scores[:, 1]                 # where the units sit on the first component
feature_contributions(m, 1)    # which feature drives it
```

### References
`measure = :moran` is equation (21) of Krzyśko, M., Nijkamp, P., Ratajczak,
W., Wołyński, W. & Wenerska, B. (2024). Spatio-temporal principal component
analysis. *Spatial Economic Analysis*, 19(1), 8–29, with the symmetrisation
of its equation (23).

`measure = :geary` is equation (4) of Krzyśko, M., Nijkamp, P., Ratajczak,
W., Wołyński, W., Wojtyła, A. & Wenerska, B. (2023). A novel spatio-temporal
principal component analysis based on Geary's contiguity ratio. *Computers,
Environment and Urban Systems*, 103, 101980.

Both rest on the spatial PCA of Jombart, T., Devillard, S., Dufour, A.-B. &
Pontier, D. (2008). Revealing cryptic spatial patterns in genetic variability
by a new multivariate method. *Heredity*, 101, 92–103, and on the
multivariate functional PCA of Górecki et al. (2018).
